author: Fraser Needham
title: ISC minister says she was not expecting Kinew’s comments about abolishing the Indian Act
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she was as surprised as anyone when Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew raised the idea of abolishing the Indian Act last month and was hoping for more information on what role the province would play.

“I think it’s interesting to see somebody who’s a provincial premier wanting to frame up that space,” she said. “Clearly, in his role he would have to indicate his responsibility in the provincial seat and how you would serve those off-reserve community members.

“I think that’s the initiative I was hoping to see as a minister coming out of that space because you have to increase the responsibility, the partnership, the role of the provincial government in the path beyond the Indian Act.”

The idea of getting rid of the Indian Act was raised by Kinew during a press conference at the First Nations First Ministers meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26.

“What you saw was a spontaneous moment where premier Kinew wanted to speak about status. Wanted to speak about the Indian Act.”

The Indian Act, passed in 1876, continues to govern matters of Indian status, First Nations governance, and reserve lands. The federal government has tried, and failed, to abolish it a number of times in the past 50 years.

title: Indigenous youth, Elders join national protests against Bill C-39 at Prime Minister’s Office
content:
Indigenous youth, Elders, environmental organizations and labour leaders rallied outside the Prime Minister’s Office Thursday as part of a national day of action against Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.




Opponents say the legislation would override Treaty rights, weaken environmental laws and expand Cabinet power to fast-track major projects.




Hand-drummers from the Ottawa River Singers opened the demonstration. 




Speakers warned the omnibus bill would give the government broad new authority to designate “regions of national interest,” suspend or amend key environmental protections, and override the inherent, Treaty and constitutionally protected rights of First Nations.




Dara Wawatie-Chabot, an Indigenous youth speaker, told the crowd the legislation threatens protections across the board.

“Bill C-39 would go right through any type of protections, whether it is environmental protections, labour protections or Indigenous rights,” she said. “They are just going to be completely bypassing all of that in order to get access to resources that are going to just make things worse for everybody on this planet.”

title: Shelter-in-place advisory issued near Squamish, B.C., due to flooding from heavy rain
content:
A shelter-in-place advisory has been issued north of Vancouver, where roads have flooded due to dam run-off triggered by storms that have drenched parts of southern British Columbia with more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours.




The rains that are forecast to ease Thursday before a weaker system arrives Friday have also forced evacuation orders for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil’wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts of the Village of Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver.




The entire Village of Pemberton is under an evacuation alert, while the District of Squamish about 90 kilometres to the south has told residents of Paradise Valley to shelter in place after dam discharge swamped local roads.




British Columbia’s emergency information system says residents in areas including Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch should stay indoors if they can.




The District of Squamish says in a statement that the spill level from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked at approximately 5 a.m. and was expected to decrease slowly throughout the day.

title: First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations

Lomax framed the scale of planned investments in transportation, energy and electricity infrastructure as “a generational opportunity for First Nations to play a leading role in building Canada’s future.”




“When First Nations move beyond participation to become owners, we create lasting economic opportunities, build wealth for future generations and strengthen Canada’s economy as a whole. When First Nations succeed, Canada succeeds,” Lomax said in a statement following the budget. 




“But we need to think beyond consultation, employment and contracting opportunities. content:

Indigenous Veterans Day ceremony

For the first time, the annual gathering incorporates traditional practice and offers participants a moment to ground themselves, reflect and honour First Nations, Inuit and Métis people who served in Canada’s military.

“There are so many people from the Indigenous communities that went into wars that a lot of people weren’t aware of,” Francoeur told

He says Indigenous people have served in conflicts throughout Canada’s military history, including the First and Second World Wars, as well as NATO and United Nations operations.




Indigenous Veterans Day is recognized across Canada on Nov. 8.

title: Australia’s inaugural Ambassador for First Nations People visits Canada
content:
Four years ago, the Australian government took a step that no other country has taken when it created the position of Ambassador for First Nations People.

The ambassador, Justin Mohamed, is a Gooreng Gooreng man from Bundaberg in Queensland.

Mohamed recently visited Canada for a series of high-level meetings with Canadian ministers, including Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty.

The ambassador also met with national Indigenous organizations and economic groups. Among the similarities between the two countries, says Mohamed, is the effort to involve Indigenous peoples in economic opportunities.

“For the first time, in my 36 years of working in Indigenous affairs, where both of our leaders are talking very positively about the uplift of economic engagement with our First peoples in our country and seeing the benefits of that,” says Mohamed on the latest episode of Face to Face.

“Obviously, here there is things that we can learn and things that Canada can learn from Australia. Our vast country, we’ve got a lot of land mass, we’ve got so many people spread across that, how to get those connections across our land and hopefully across our waters so we have more connections from country to country.”

author: Bruce De La Cruz
title: ‘Where is the accountability?’: Nunavut’s child advocate says territory’s protection issues aren’t being addressed
content:
Another scathing report from the federal auditor general looking into Nunavut’s child protection system came as no surprise to Jane Bates, the territory’s child welfare advocate.

On Nov. 3, deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes released the latest in a series of damning reports outlining how Nunavut is failing to protect Inuit children in care of the state.

For Bates, who has already written extensively about the issue, it came as no surprise.

“These concerns have been reported on, recommendations have been made about them, and yet they remain unaddressed to the detriment of children, youth, and families,” Bates told APTN News, “which is really the fundamental issue that everyone should be really concerned about, is the lack of follow through.

“We’re not talking about buildings. We’re not talking about bicycles. We’re talking about children and youth and their families. And so it’s deeply concerning.”

Hayes’ report outlined found that “fundamental weaknesses” in Nunavut’s child welfare system and its handling of the territory’s most vulnerable “remain unresolved” in audits going back to 2011.

“When children are removed from their homes and are placed in foster care for protection, the department takes on responsibility for their safety and well being,” Hayes said at a news conference on Nov. 3. “Yet it could not consistently demonstrate that basic safeguards, intended to protect children and place them in safe environments, were being followed.”

According to the latest report, approximately 400 children and youth are in Nunavut’s foster care system; the majority are Inuit.

Hayes said his office reviewed 40 cases and found issues that go back more than a decade.

The major concerns included that Nunavut’s Department of Family Services didn’t maintain required monthly in-person contact in more than 90 per cent of the cases; only performed 52 per cent of required evaluations for home safety” and, in 75 per cent of the cases, failed to give important information about a child to caregivers.

“Where is the accountability here? And again, we’re hearing, ‘oh, yes, we accept all the recommendations and we’re going to make changes.’ Where have you been? This has been upwards of 15 years. And we shouldn’t still be having this conversation.”

One Inuk family services employee who spoke to APTN News on condition that we grant anonymity, said the lack of Inuit staffing is the biggest concern.

“There’s like 30 per cent Inuit employed by this department,” the employee said. “I think if we had an Inuk supervisor, it would make a difference. Someone who knows the culture.”

Clayton Greaves, assistant deputy minister of Family Services Wellness Division, oversees the operations for the child welfare system in Nunavut.

“When I reviewed the report, and I hear what’s happening, we accept the other general recommendations and we accept that there’s work that’s in front of us that we have to do,” he said.

Greaves emphasized the challenges in running the child welfare system and said they’re doing the best with what they have.

“When we look at the report, we have to be careful that we don’t draw the conclusion that the gaps that we see is directly related to children being harmed,” he said. “And I wanted to make sure that we’re able to emphasize that. Yes, there are challenges with our new information system. We recognize and accept, you know, the recommendation, like I said, from what the Auditor General reported.”

Auditor general funds Nunavut foster care continues to fail vulnerable children

According to Bates’ own report that was filed in September, harm is coming to children.

“In the Reviews of Critical Injuries and Deaths program, reports of sexualized violence increased significantly, from eight in 2024–2025 to 22 in 2025–2026, while the number of young people who died by suicide tragically increased to 13,” she wrote in a report tabled in the Nunavut legislature.

“Children and youth who grow up in care, there’s been numerous studies done on the trajectory for young people,” she told APTN. “The outcomes are not good for children who grow up in care. They’re away from their families. They’re away from their culture. They lose their language.

“Children have the right to grow up with their families. They have a right to be protected. These are their fundamental rights under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. And currently, in Nunavut, that is not happening.”

Bruce was thrilled to join APTN on a 10-month contract in Yellowknife, where he’s working as a video journalist. Before moving to Yellowknife, he worked in civic journalism in townships east of Ottawa, Ottawa’s AV industry as a Technician/Camera Operator, and as the On-Camera Talent of his alma mater’s Digital TV Channel (Conestoga College Digital TV), which was launched in January 2024 on Roku TV, and later Apple TV.

title: Grieving mother livestreams private Manitoba police watchdog meeting to force transparency
content:
A grieving mother is taking transparency into her own hands by livestreaming meetings with Manitoba’s police watchdog and justice minister over the lack of independent investigation into her daughter’s violent arrest and subsequent death.




Crystal Delvenne said she chose to livestream the meetings to Facebook because she’s “lost trust in these systems” over the last few months following the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba’s (IIU) refusal to investigate an arrest by the Brandon Police Service (BPS).




Crystal’s daughter Cassity told her police beat her during the June 12 arrest, leaving her with bruised ribs, bleeding ears and hearing loss.




Cassity was found dead in her apartment of an unknown cause nine days later. Police said Cassity’s death is unrelated to her arrest.




On Friday, BPS announced it concluded its investigation into her death, saying a “definitive cause of death has been determined,” but added it could not share it publicly due to privacy laws and out of respect for the family.




According to the family, nothing has been received at the time this story was published.




Still, Crystal has many questions regarding her daughter’s case and the IIU’s operations. She said the IJF’s reporting on the IIU’s

 following its investigations into officer-involved deaths pushed her to get answers.

title: On the Outside: Is Manitoba contributing to its own crime problem?
content:

This is where she is dropped off every time she gets released from the Women’s Correctional Centre in the nearby town of Headingley.




“I’ve been doing this my whole life,” she said, as she waits for the bus that will take her straight downtown.




“I’ve been in and out of jail every year since I was 12.”




Being left on the outskirts of the city, without a plan and with nothing more than a bus ticket and the clothes they were arrested in, is a common story for people exiting Manitoba’s provincial correctional system.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Prime minister announces $1B for housing, new hospital to ‘tackle’ homelessness in Winnipeg
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney joined Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and the mayor of Winnipeg to announce a joint funding venture to build more than 2,000 new homes and an addictions treatment centre in the middle province’s capital.

The federal government will be allocating $1 billion overall, with $800 million going to the homes and the remaining $200 million going to the proposed Winnipeg Mental Health and Addictions Centre, as well as the refurbishment of similar facilities.

“There’s no simple answer,” Carney said. “This is a hard problem. And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short.”

Funds will also go to supporting local, grassroots organizations that are already involved in addressing the homelessness crisis, including End Homelessness Winnipeg, the North End Women’s Centre, and Chalmers Neighbourhood Renewal Corporation.

Carney said the partnership is one project in an “unprecedented” $30 billion allocation in the 2026 budget, with the end goal of ending homelessness in Canada in 10 years.

“Help works,” he said, which extends to housing and healthcare.

Alongside federal, provincial and municipal governments, funding for these Winnipeg-based projects will also be provided by First Nation governments such as the Southern Chiefs’ Organization (SCO), as well as private funders such as True North Sports and Entertainment, owner of the Winnipeg Jets and the primary investor in several major infrastructure projects downtown.

“It’s the first time in our country’s history where every level of government has come together to tackle homelessness,” Kinew said. “Including First Nations and Métis governments.”

“The reality is that a huge part of what we see is that [in the past] failed policies like residential schools left a disproportionate number of Indigenous people vulnerable to the ravages of addictions. And the only way for us to find a solution is to have the full participation and engagement of the leaders of those people.”

He said, “A challenge for Indigenous Peoples in Canada has never been that Indigenous Peoples don’t know the solutions. Absolutely we do. The challenge has been that we didn’t have access to the resources and to the decision-making tables to make that happen.”

Carney said that previous government and community efforts to address homelessness have been “inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated, and not sustained.”

He said it’s “imperative” that this new strategy succeeds.”

“In Canada, we know we’re not perfect, but we always strive to be good,” Carney said. “We do things because they’re right, not because they’re easy. Ending homelessness is hard; it’s good, and it’s right. And it will require more than compassion.

“It will require ambition, execution, and partnership amongst all levels of government with contributions from philanthropy and business,” Carney added.

There was no determined answer when it came to where most of the 2,000 planned units will be built, but the first 373 are currently being developed inside of Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, formerly known as the Hudson’s Bay Building, just down the street from the Manitoba Legislature.

The building was acquired by the SCO in 2022, and is scheduled to be complete in 2028. Funding is supported through a partnership with True North.

Jamil Mahmood, the executive director of Main Street Project, a major non-profit addictions treatment centre and homeless shelter, said that additional housing would be useful anywhere in the downtown core.

The organization’s emergency shelter on Main Street has been affected by several fires in 2026, beginning in January. The most recent was on Oct. 31.

Money from this announcement will help refurbish the building, which housed over 2,900 people in 2025, according to its annual report.

“We know that’s where people are, we know that’s where the resources are, so the more you can put housing up where resources are is great,” he said.

“I think over time we can definitely expand that … from the core area to different areas, but then you also need to move resources to those places,” he added. “So we believe a decentralized model would work over time, but right now we have resources downtown.”

Mahmood said “the big thing,” however, is the inclusion of wrap-around support on-site, and staff who can remain there to help.

“I think that helps a lot of people really feel more comfortable with this housing,” he said. “And also, the reverse option is people stay in encampments or they stay on street corners.”

End Homelessness Winnipeg, a non-profit that, through its data collection, determined that every one in four homeless people in Winnipeg is Indigenous, stated the announcement was a “significant opportunity for Winnipeg,” after the fact.

“We have an opportunity to move beyond managing homelessness and toward ending it,” CEO Jennifer Moore Rattray said in the statement. “Housing is medicine, but housing alone is not enough. We need prevention, mental wellness services and sustained community supports.”

Similar to Mahmood’s point, Moore Rattray also noted that “the solutions are already in our communities, led by people and organizations who know what works.

“This once-in-a-lifetime investment could give us the resources to bring those solutions to scale and create lasting change for the people we serve.”

The additional money going towards mental health care would be to help address the issues which may render someone homeless at their source, Carney said.

Now not everyone without a home needs health care, but most desperately do,” he said. “Nine in 10 people on the Winnipeg streets face a health challenge, most often addiction, mental illness or both. And for them, the emergency room becomes their only respite, but it’s a temporary respite. They’re treated, discharged, and then they go straight back onto the street. and the cycle begins again.”

As of Friday afternoon, the wait time at St. Boniface Hospital’s emergency room was 15 hours long, according to the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority.

He said having improved mental health care would decrease the number of people visiting emergency rooms as a last resort.

In Toronto, Carney added, emergency room visits went down 80 per cent because of the Fred Victor Dunn House, a four-storey apartment building with on-site social support for people who were previously homeless or struggling with addiction. A new mental health centre in Winnipeg would fill the same need.

Kinew described the centre as “a new health care campus” and said that Manitoba has needed to “do more” when it comes to mental health and addictions support, and not only for the homeless population.

“I want to be clear,” he added, “yes, there’s a lot of people we drive by on the street doing the fentanyl fold, but there’s people in the suburbs in a basement who are struggling right now, there’s people in rural communities who are struggling from the very same vices and very same disease, and this service is going to be there for everybody in Manitoba who wants recovery.”

Mark Chipman, the executive chairman of True North, had originally proposed the idea of a new hospital, according to Kinew.

Alongside Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, True North is also responsible for the $650 million redevelopment of Portage Place Shopping Mall, soon-to-be the site of a mixed-use True North Campus, which will include housing, health care centre, grocery store, and urban greenspaces.

Chipman said the number of people “with an acquired brain injury” due to toxic drugs “is staggering,” and the new centre will serve as “an entry point to stabilise them, and then find the correct supports for them.

“Every person’s got a different story, and then those supports are co-located and lined up,” he said.

Speaking at the podium, Chipman said he’s learned that “there are several ways to look at this [homelessness] crisis.

“You can look at the burden it places on our health care system, our social service network, our justice system, and the sheer human impact it has on those in our emergency rooms and our first responders. You can look at it through the effect it has on our community’s sense of safety and security,” he said.

The stop in Winnipeg was the first of several in a tour Carney is taking to promote the 2026 federal budget, according to the Canadian Press.

APTN also asked SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels for a comment, but a spokesperson said he is not speaking to media at this time.

title: InFocus: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s declaration on abolishing the Indian Act an ‘absurd distraction’

At the noon break at the First Nations First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew quoted to Karl Marx as he forwarded his call to action.




“Abolish the 

Indian Act

,” Kinew said. “You have nothing to lose but your chains.”




This week on APTN News InFocus, our guests Pam Palmater and Veldon Coburn argue First Nations have much to lose.




“There are thousands of bylaws and codes, and other laws that First Nations have passed to govern their communities under the Indian Act that have to be addressed,” said Palmater, a lawyer and chair in Indigenous Governance at Toronto Metropolitan University. “All of these things are constitutionally protected.




“So, you literally cannot say, ‘Hey, let’s just abolish it’. That alone, dealing with that intricate web of laws and constitutional issues, that’s going to take a long, long time.”




Canadian leaders have been toying with abolishing or amending the Indian Act for more than 70 years.




As Palmater notes, there’s a pattern.




“During the 1969 White Paper, you had [former prime minister] Pierre Elliot Trudeau who wanted to make Canada self-sufficient in oil and gas. That was his big agenda item,” Palmater said. “All of a sudden, well, Treaty rights might stand in the way, and First Nations, so let’s get rid of the Indian Act.”

content:
The 2026 U.S. midterms resulted in several firsts, including the victories of Peggy Flanagan and Deb Haaland, the first Indigenous women to serve as state senator and governor, respectively, in the country’s history.




“My ancestors came to the Rio Grande Valley in the late 1200s, and this beautiful land has sustained all of us for generations,” Haaland said in her victory speech Tuesday night. “Just off this road, my grandmother was taken to boarding school, and along with my grandfather, survived through a time when the federal government attempted to strip them of their languages, traditions and identities. Yet, we are still here.”




Although the results have not been finalized, the Democrats have been favoured to win the U.S. House of Representatives (236 seats to 129) and Senate (54 to 44), a sweeping result which flipped 29 seats from red to blue, as of Wednesday afternoon.




Midterm elections are held two years after a presidential election. All members of Congress, also called the House of Representatives, are up for election, and 33 of the Senate’s 100 seats were up for grabs.




Alongside Flanagan (Minnesota) and Haaland (New Mexico), the midterms also brought in Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator in Michigan; Chris Pappas, the first openly gay senator in New Hampshire; and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in Georgia.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: AFN, other defendants delaying lawsuit by former national chief, lawyer says
content:
It has been five months since a judge issued a court order requiring the Assembly of First Nations and the other parties named in a lawsuit by former national chief RoseAnne Archibald to produce their documents by July 31.

Nearly three months later, Archibald’s lawyer says they’re still waiting.

David Shiller said the AFN and the other parties remain in breach of that order, forcing the matter back before the court for another case conference and another delay.

“Oral examination for discovery (was to) occur, between November second and November 9th,” Shiller said in an interview with APTN News. He added that they’ve still not received the required documents. On July 31, 2026, what they delivered to me was what they called a draft affidavit of documents, and it was only purporting to be from the AFN.

“There was nothing delivered on behalf of the individual defendants who were the individual members of the executive committee.”

The affidavit of documents is a form that comes from the court that discloses relevant evidence related to a case.

“What they delivered was a document that says ‘I, blank, of the town of blank, in the county of blank, affirm I am the blank, of the Assembly of First Nations.’ It wasn’t a sworn affidavit of documents. It was a draft,” Shiller said. “And that’s not just a technical difference. The whole point of making each side swear an affidavit is to get them to tell the other side and the court that they have done a diligent search of their records.

APTN reached out to AFN for comment and received a statement that said it can’t comment on a legal case but that the organization ”remains committed to meeting its legal obligations to the courts.”

Archibald launched the lawsuit June 14, 2022, naming the regional chiefs of the AFN at the time of her dismissal. Those regional chiefs include Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, Paul Prosper, Ghislain Picard, Glen Hare, Joanne Bernard, Kluane Adamek, Terry Teegee, Bobby Cameron, Darlene Bernard, Junior Gould and Gerald Antoine.

Woodhouse Nepinak is now the national chief, Prosper is a sitting senator, while Picard and Bernard are retired.

She also named the AFN as a whole, as well as the National Indian Brotherhood and the executive committee comprised of the regional chiefs.

Archibald is seeking damages of $5 million for “breach of contract and oppression; indemnity for the legal fees incurred by the plaintiff from July, 2021 through June, 2022 in connection with the campaign to sideline her and oust her from the Assembly of First Nations,” according to the statement of claim.

She is also seeking the legal fees she incurred in order to respond to her “unlawful suspension of her employment and the unlawful prohibition imposed on her by the Executive Committee of the Assembly of First Nations in connection with the 2022 Annual General Assembly and the Chiefs and Assembly meetings,” according to the statement of claim.

In its statement of defence, filed in Ontario Superior Court on Feb. 6, 2026, the AFN and the other defendants said they “deny each and every allegation contained in the Statement of Claim…” and that “the relief sought in paragraph 1 of the statement of claim is grossly excessive, exaggerated, inflated, and too remote and not commensurate with any losses, damages, or expenses, if any, sustained by the Plaintiff.”

The statement also said the defendants specifically deny that they initiated or engaged in any campaign of retaliation against Archibald and they have “no knowledge of any campaign to sideline and oust” Archibald from the Assembly of First Nations and that she must offer “strict proof” of the allegation.

They also deny that the defendants conspired to trigger workplace-harassment complaints against the plaintiff and also denies that the four complaints themselves were part of any conspiracy and that the Executive Committee exceeded its jurisdiction… or that there was an abuse of power by the Executive Committee as alleged.”

Archibald served as the AFN regional chief for Ontario from 2018 until she ran for national chief and won in 2021. She butted heads with then national chief Perry Bellegarde over “serious issues regarding the way the AFN and the Executive Committee were run,” according to her statement of claim.

Shiller said the fact that the AFN only provided a draft affidavit not signed by anyone means that that Archibald doesn’t have the “comfort of an oath that the proper search has been done. And looking at the documents that they listed in their draft, it supports the assertion that a proper search was not done.”

Just ten documents were produced by the AFN, according to Shiller.

“Doing a quick review of the ten, right away I see that one document is clearly missing. That’s the June 17, 2022 letter from Paul Prosper of the executive committee to the national chief saying that she’s suspended,” Shiller said. “Well, this whole case is about the steps taken by the executive committee to derail the national chief’s agenda. And certainly that suspension is a central part of what we say is a campaign to derail her platform.”

Shiller noted that there are no emails listed between the executive committee members and other people within the AFN regarding the actions taken against the national chief.

“Those things are clearly relevant and have not been produced. (AFN) Counsel has advised me that, she is still reviewing the emails. So, the fact that there’s some review going on now tells me that there are emails that might be relevant, and they haven’t been produced,” Shiller said.

During the November hearings, Shiller said the rules give each side only seven hours of examination.

“So, you know, here we are. We don’t want to be asking questions about documents we don’t have. We don’t want to be going there and saying, can you produce this document and that document? It should have been done already,” Shiller said.

The delay has necessitated another case conference with possible dates provided by the court in November.

Shiller said Archibald remains steadfast.

“And, you know, she’s patient. She’d rather not have these delays, but the delays are not going to make her go away,” Shiller said.

Archibald posted an update on social media on Oct. 21, writing in part:

“…I have nothing to hide. I put my allegations on the public record and shared my court documents for anyone to read. I am prepared to have the evidence examined, and I will see this process through. The AFN should be equally prepared.”

“Over the past year, I’ve heard from community members across many Nations who want the same things: truth, transparency and accountability from those in leadership,” Archibald continued.

“That is not asking too much. It is what our people deserve from anyone entrusted to lead. And when our questions remain unanswered, we keep asking.”

title: AFN presses Ottawa for funded plan to close $376B infrastructure gap in upcoming federal budget
content:

“The AFN estimates put the First Nations infrastructure gap at over $376 billion over the next ten years. Canada committed to closing this gap by 2030. The budget must set out a funded plan with First Nations to deliver on that commitment,” she said.

Woodhouse Nepinak pointed to joint research with the Conference Board of Canada showing the economic payoff of those investments.

“Through our research with the Conference Board of Canada, the Assembly of First Nations describes how these generational investments will create hundreds of thousands of jobs and return $1.82 for every one dollar invested in closing the gap,” she said.

Face to Face

title: Cody Drygeese makes history as Yellowknife swears in new mayor and council
content:
Cody Drygeese held his drum as he swore to serve the city of Yellowknife for the next four years. It was a proud moment with family in attendance, including both of his grandmothers.




The newly elected councillor is a member of the Yellowknives Dene First Nation, and is believed to be the first person from the First Nation elected to the position.




“I asked if I could swear my oath of office over my drum and they said okay,” Drygeese told 

APTN News

 following Monday’s ceremony.

title: St’át’imc Chiefs Council challenges Ottawa’s pipeline plans in court
content:
A group of First Nations in British Columbia announced they have filed a federal court application for a judicial review of the federal government’s decision to fast-track the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta and BC as a “project of national interest.” In a press conference held in Richmond B.C. this morning, members of the St’át’imc Chiefs Council — representing eleven Nations of the St’át’imc people (also known as Lilloee) —decried what they called a lack of consultation and stressed the need for the courts to slow the developmental process.

Chief Bonnie Adolph of the Sekw’el’was (Cayoose Creek) First Nation began by outlining threats to the salmon upon which her people rely. She said that when her community wrote to the Major Projects Office asking to be consulted about listing the project under the Build Canada Act, they were told since their land was not on the proposed pipeline route, the Crown would not consult with them.

“When we told the Major Projects Office their narrow geographic approach failed to account for downstream, interconnected and cumulative environmental risks to our inherent St’át’imc title and rights,” Adolph said, “We were told that we could send comments like any member of the public, but not as a First Nation whom the Crown had a legal [duty] to consult. This is not lawful, this is not constitutional, this is not consistent with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People.”

The salmon central to the lives of St’át’imc people are all over the waters threatened by an oil spill from the pipeline, said Chief Travis Peters from N’Quatqua (Anderson Lake) First Nation.

“The salmon we rely upon travel the Fraser Estuary and the Fraser River twice,” he explained. “Once, as juveniles heading out to the ocean, and [again] as adults returning home to spawn. There are salmon in the river system almost all year. The idea of the construction of new crude oil infrastructure in the heart of the Fraser River Estuary on unstable soil is terrifying.

“What happens if there’s an earthquake? What happens if the pipeline leaks? What happens if the tankers run aground?”

Peters noted that 100 First Nations signed the 2010 Save the Fraser Declaration, but “if anything, the health of the Fraser River salmon has only worsened since 2010. The cumulative impacts of climate change and development have become more severe.”

Chief Justin Kane from Ts’kw’aylaxw First Nation (formerly Pavilion Indian Band), who is also Chair for the St’át’imc Chiefs Council, said the Chiefs Council filed for a judicial review because the federal court failed to meet its constitutional duties to St’át’imc.

“We know this project could have serious, potentially catastrophic risks for our fishing rights and way of life,” he told media. “Salmon is part of who we are. It’s part of our identity. And we have the right to understand what those risks are and to be immediately consulted about whether they are actually working.”

The federal government forced the Chiefs’ hands, Kane said, by insisting that the only question is how — and not if — the project will go ahead.

“If this decision is not challenged in court,” Kane argued, “it sets a dangerous precedent all Canadians should be concerned about. It is foolhardy for the government to try to push through a project at breakneck speed without proper assessment and consultation. Canada is attempting to circumvent its own laws, and ours.”

He said Ottawa has said it would consult with First Nations later, despite the fact that the project is moving ahead.

“Because the Pacific Link is listed under the Building Canada Act,” he said, “the Act says it must be granted a conditional document that is deemed to be all environmental approvals for the project. How can the future of consultation be meaningful if the decision is already made?”

Hugh Braker is a member of Tseshaht First Nation on Vancouver Island as well as of the First Nations Summit Political Executive.

In his statement to media, Braker noted that Mark Carney has said repeatedly that taking action to protect against climate change is “a moral duty.”

“Those were his words,” Braker said. “And what’s he doing about it? He’s building a pipeline. Probably the worst thing he could do. Our prime minister wears a coat of hypocrisy. And he has to realize that. He has to realize that things like life expectancy are going down because of climate change.”

Braker added that First Nations have already issued a climate-change document (the BC First Nations Climate Strategy and Action Plan) that the province of British Columbia has adopted.

“But here comes the pipeline,” Braker said. “So really, there needs to be a solid answer from the prime minister, why he said that everyone has a moral duty when it comes to climate change, but he apparently is exempt. I need to hear from him why that is.”

BC Assembly of First Nations Regional Chief Terry Teegee noted the importance of speaking up not only about the Pacific Link pipeline, but also Bill C-39, Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act and the Building Canada Strong Act.

“I had the opportunity to present to the many Senators our concerns of an untenable review process of one project, one review, one year,” Teegee said. “It bypasses the meaning of what consultation is, the meaning of the United Nations Declaration Act and free, prior and informed consent. This project being pre-approved does not meet the standard of not only a free, prior and informed consent, but the minimum standard of consultation.”

In the near future, Teegee predicted, conflict between First Nations and the federal government will escalate.

“And it’s not just First Nations,” he said. “It’s the unions that I’ve seen that are developing a war room. It’s the youth that are raising their voices about climate change. It’s many of our First Nations here in British Columbia that are concerned about not only the environment, but also the minimum standards of the [provincial] Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, and also the United Nations Declaration Act federally.”

Grand Chief Stewart Phillip (Sylix Nation) of the Union of BC Indian Chiefs decried political and social attitudes dismissive of Indigenous rights and title.

“Canadians and British Columbians absolutely refuse to recognize our rights,” he said, “our rights that are international in nature, that are enshrined in the Constitution and have been upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada on so many different occasions. Yet Canadians still have this backward, ignorant notion that somehow that’s not important, that’s not real.”

Phillip framed the Pacific Link as a project created in partnership between Prime Minister Carney and Alberta premier Danielle Smith.

“It’s the same pipeline that we fought with Enbridge and Kinder Morgan,” he argued, “just a different location. So again, my fundamental basic message to the corporations is buyers beware when you invest in British Columbia, because we’re not standing down. We’re not stepping back. We have the colour of right on our side inherently, constitutionally and legally. And we’ll be back in the courtrooms again.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
content:
British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he also warned of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.







Doerkson made the comments as newly elected Conservatives gathered for their first caucus meeting on Monday, where he told them that their job now is to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.




He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.




“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”




He said that B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every single time.




Doerkson said people will be watching to see if his caucus will splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

title: First Nations in B.C., environmental group call out foreign investment in liquid natural gas
content:
An announcement by the Mitsubishi Corporation (MC) Monday, which says it will partner with Blackstone Credit & Insurance in its liquefaction infrastructure holding company for the LNG Canada project in British Columbia, isn’t sitting well with some First Nations and environmental groups.

The transaction is valued at approximately US$1.6 billion.

“By investing billions in LNG Canada through American private equity funds, four of Canada’s largest pension funds have ignored their core obligations to their contributors and beneficiaries,” said Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health. The charitable organization works to protect pensions and the climate by bringing together beneficiaries and their pension funds to engage on the climate crisis.

“These pension funds are gambling their own members’ retirement savings on a high-risk, highly-polluting LNG facility that’s harming local residents and contributing to catastrophic climate change,” a news release from the group said.

On Monday, an investor consortium led by Blackstone, in partnership with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System (OMERS), Investment Management Corporation of Ontario (IMCO) and Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP), announced that it would invest billions to acquire a 49.9% stake in a Mitsubishi Corporation (MC) subsidiary that holds MC’s stake in LNG Canada – a giant liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal near Kitimat, British Columbia (BC).

Shift said the LNG industry is “already propped up by generous public subsidies and tax shields in Canada, (and) is now relying on billions of dollars invested from Canadian workers and their retirement savings” to support the project.

The group said LNG Canada is a “high-carbon project that has been plagued by severe and ongoing operating issues. It is estimated that LNG Canada flared more gas in 2025 than any other facility in the world.”

Natural gas flaring is the controlled burning of waste or excess natural gas through a flare stack or boom at oil and gas extraction sites, refineries, and processing plants.

Among the environmental affects, it produces black carbon particles that settle on ice and snow, accelerating Arctic melt and regional warming.

The group also stated that New York-based Blackstone Inc has likely expanded its ownership into LNG Canada, and already holds existing ownership in Ksi Lisims LNG, Canada’s two largest liquefied natural gas projects.

Ksi Lisims LNG is a proposed floating natural gas liquefaction production, storage, and offloading facility with a marine terminal located on the north coast of British Columbia. Prime Minister Mark Carney referred Ksi Lisims LNG to the Major Projects Office on Nov. 13, 2025.

The project referral also includes the 800-kilometre Prince Rupert Gas Transmission Project to supply feed gas for liquefaction, and a 95-kilometre electrical transmission line to supply electricity to the facility.

“As Indigenous Peoples, we follow our LAW to protect Land, Air, Water, all humans depend on these. These projects destroy our law – yet our pension funds are choosing to ignore our laws and our rights when investing in LNG Canada,” said Chief Na’Moks, Hereditary Chief of the Tsayu (Beaver Clan) of the Wet’suwet’en Nation.

“Just last month, I spoke to the CPP executives about the lack of consent for major parts of this project, and they heard overwhelmingly from other pension members and beneficiaries that we do not want our hard-earned dollars to be invested in oil and gas projects that are destroying our climate,” Chief Na’Moks said.

“Why are they choosing to ignore Indigenous leaders and a clear chorus of voices who are opposed to this move. Why would we allow this?”

On October 6, Indigenous leaders and health and environmental groups also hold a news conference on Parliament Hill to announce a challenge over Export Development Canada’s financing of maritime liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure.

In April 2026, it was revealed that LNG Canada has been excessively flaring up to an average of 40 times more gas than its permits allow and continues to experience ongoing operational issues due to a defect in the main flare stack.

The groups also emphasize that LNG Canada’s expansion modules will be built in China, and Ksi Lisims LNG’s modules by Samsung Heavy Industries in South Korea, and claim both projects’ primary economic benefits will not remain in Canada.

Blackstone holds ownership in Ksi Lisims LNG through a private equity placement into Texas-based Western LNG, which is “the entity that will construct, own and operate the assets of the Project,” according to the province of B.C.

The groups further noted that Blackstone founder, Chairman and CEO is multi-billionaire Stephen Schwarzman, who is an informal advisor and close ally to United States President Donald Trump.

Leanne has a certificate in broadcasting and has more than 12 years of radio news experience, both as an anchor and reporter in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Métis journalist is a passionate writer and born storyteller and loves to connect with people and learn about their life experiences.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Feds declare Roberts Bank 2 expansion ‘project of national interest’
content:
A large-scale port expansion to be located off the coast of Delta, B.C., has been labelled as a ‘project of national interest,’ a designation which, according to environmental advocates, could result in the extinction of the Southern Resident Killer Whales.

In an email sent to APTN News on the heels of the announcement, Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate at Environmental Defence, wrote that not only is this “bad news for orcas,” but that it may be “a run-around on the Species at Risk Act, given that was the only approval that the project didn’t have.”

Robert Banks Terminal 2 is an expansion of the Port of Vancouver, operated by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority (VFPA) and located on 130 hectares (about 200 soccer pitches) of marine land off the B.C. coast.

According to a release from Ottawa, the project would add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity, increasing it by “approximately 50 per cent.”

It would also support “up to $100 billion in annual trade,” therefore “helping Canada achieve its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035.”

It meets the criteria of what can be considered a project in the national interest, according to Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act, which are that it must “strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security”; “provide economic or other benefits”; “advance the interests of Indigenous Peoples”; and “contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives.”

Once this criteria is met, major projects may be exempt from certain laws, such as the Species at Risk Act.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that, “By listing Roberts Bank Terminal 2 as a project of national interest, we are better connecting our economy with the world and diversifying our trade. As the world competes for capital, Canada will not wait. We are building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive Canadian economy.”

However, the project is also slated to be built in the Fraser River Estuary, which has already lost more than 85 per cent of floodplain habitat and supports 102 species at risk, according to Levin.

“The estuary is critical habitat for salmon and SRKW, southern resident killer whales, as confirmed by DFO and the environmental assessment of the project – which assessed that the new terminal would result in destruction of the legally protected Southern Resident Killer Whale’s critical habitat,” she wrote.

A 2020 environmental assessment for the project determined that it would cause “significant adverse environmental effects” on Chinook salmon, wetlands, and the resident whales, which have been listed as critically endangered since 2003.

An application for a Species at Risk permit, which would allow the building of the Roberts Bank 2 port in the habitat, was filed on Oct. 28, 2024, with a deadline of Oct. 28, 2026 — two days ago, as of publishing.

‘An incredible animal’: B.C. port expansion could drive southern resident killer whales to extinction, advocates warn

As of Friday morning, the tool used to track the permit’s progress on Canada’s website indicated it was overdue, but by the afternoon, the page had been wiped.

Canada held a consultation period while it considered the national interest designation, which began

In a letter sent to the Major Projects Office by Raincoast Conservation Foundation, the advocacy and research organization wrote that “Designation as a PONI is not an appropriate use of the Building Canada Act.

“Raincoast is concerned that the national interest cannot be reduced to container capacity, trade volume and construction speed when the proposal is in the Fraser River Estuary. Promises and investments announced by the federal government … to ensure prosperity by combining regulatory certainty with environmental protection are an insufficient guarantee given the level of harm identified from this project.”

Levin stated that, “by declaring this mega-port as a ‘project of national interest,’ Prime Minister Carney has dealt a devastating blow to the last remaining Southern Resident Killer Whales.

“This political moment will pass, but extinction is forever.”

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Family of Miranda Mamakwa seeking criminal investigation into ‘negligent’ death of mother
content:
The family of a woman who died after a federal program did not arrange transportation to medical appointments is asking for a criminal investigation.

“The criminal justice system should only be invoked where grounds exist to believe a crime has been committed,” read the statement from the family. “Public officials are as accountable as anyone else in this country for reckless acts that endanger those in their charge.”

According to her family, Miranda Mamakwa died on Sept. 8 after she didn’t receive transportation to multiple important appointments following an open-heart surgery.

She was 31 and the mother of three kids.

“Literally, the blood of Indigenous people is required for any kind of meaningful change,” said Julian Falconer, legal counsel for the family. “We have created a pattern of behavior where we only get their attention once they [Canada] have killed somebody.”

Mamakwa was a member of Fort Severn First Nation, the northernmost community in Ontario, and was relying on transportation from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program (NIHB) to get to follow-up appointments in Thunder Bay after her surgery in April 2026.

NIHB is a federal program provided by Indigenous Services Canada (ISC), and is mandated to provide medical transportation services, alongside other supports such as medication and vision care, to First Nations and Inuit people.

Her first appointment following her return home was scheduled for May 28, and the local nursing station had sent a request by fax (the only method of communication with NIHB offices available to them, Falconer confirmed) for NIHB to provide transportation.

However, the nearest office, located in Sioux Lookout, never got back to them.

Despite multiple requests and letters from her doctor, she missed four appointments, including “an appointment with a vascular surgeon about blood clots,” according to the backgrounder provided to the media.

The backgrounder also stated that, following the surgery, Mamakwa had been put on blood thinner medication for blood clots, and was visiting the Nation’s nursing station once a week for blood work.

She eventually became lethargic and “began to lose feeling in her fingers,” the backgrounder noted, and she ultimately died of a brain haemorrhage after being transported to Thunder Bay.

Brain haemorrhages are caused by a blood vessel leaking or bursting in the brain, essentially drowning it.

Prior to her death, on Aug. 19, Mamakwa had made a grim post on social media: “If I die, please go after them.”

On Friday, Falconer and Mamakwa’s parents, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, issued a statement announcing they had sent a formal request to Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner Thomas Carrique.

“The wanton and reckless disregard shown for Miranda’s health, and ultimately her life, by those public officials responsible for arranging her medical transportation makes such an investigation a necessity,” the statement said.

Eva and Mike are staying out of the public eye, but did comment in the statement.

“This should never have happened to Miranda. She should be alive today,” they said. “We deserve to know how something like this happened, and we want the individual or individuals responsible for failing to respond to these urgent requests for transportation to be held accountable. They cost Miranda her life. They cost her children a future without their mother.”

Mother of First Nations woman who couldn’t get medical transport and died seeks reform

Falconer said he does not take criminal cases lightly, but that this circumstance was “wonton neglect.”

“Three children are without a mother. A grandmother is left explaining to these children where their mother is. Words cannot describe the extent of the neglect here,” he said.

It’s also indicative of Canada’s failure to act in the best interests of Indigenous Peoples, he said.

Alongside this matter, the lawyer is also legal counsel to a coalition of several First Nations and tribal councils, led by Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council, and Windigo First Nations Council, which filed a human rights complaint against ISC on Oct. 1.

“The complaint alleges widespread neglect and systemic discrimination by the NIHB, whose routine administrative failures effectively deny life-sustaining healthcare to remote, fly-in communities,” stated a release on the Falconers legal practice’s website.

The coalition is seeking “sweeping structural overhauls,” as well as $20,000 in damages for those who missed medical appointments, and an additional $20,000 in “compensation for damages due to Canada’s willful and reckless conduct.”

Similar to Mamakwa’s case, members of Wummumin Lake, a fly-in community with no full-time doctor, “were subject to 147 missed medical appointments between March 2025 and March 2026 alone,” because of NIHB not arranging transportation, according to Falconer.

He said this would not happen in a place like Toronto.

“They are captive to the system that’s in place and the system is supposed to be in place to honour Treaty promises,” he said. “And we have benefited through privilege and wealth from these Treaties.

“Now what we’re seeing is basically a collapse of the medical responsibility that Canada bears. And what’s outrageous about all of this is that rest assured, if a failure of this kind happened to a white family, you can absolutely be assured there would be a criminal investigation.”

Internal review underway, stated ISC

According to a statement sent to APTN News, ISC has been in the process of “reviewing the circumstances of [Mamakwa’s] passing” since Sept. 11.

This was in part due to requests for an investigation from the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority (SLFNHA) and leadership from Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN), which represents 49 First Nations in Ontario, the statement read.

“A dedicated team has been established by ISC to conduct the review,” ISC spokesperson Carolane Gratton wrote. “Guided by an ISC Patient Safety facilitator, the team will conduct interviews and discussions to map relevant interactions and identify all contributing factors, both internal and external. The team will invite input from Ms. Mamakwa’s family and others involved in her circle of care as part of the review process and the development of recommendations.”

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty also met with NAN and SLFNHA on Sept. 30, and “continues to be in open dialogue while ISC provides support,” according to the statement.

Falconer said Gull-Masty has not been in touch with Mamakwa’s family, to his knowledge.

Falconer said a review is not enough, and the case needs “serious accountability.”

“If you know of and are implicated in the deprivation of essential health services to another human, and you are paid to provide those services, and you are implicated in denying those services, you should expect to get a knock on the door from the authorities. That’s certainly the country we live in for non-Indigenous people,” he said.

title: InFocus: What’s at stake for Indigenous Peoples in the U.S. as midterm elections draw near?
content:
On Tuesday, U.S. voters will cast their ballots in the country’s midterm elections. The elections come halfway through a president’s four year term.

A record-breaking number of Indigenous candidates–at least 355–are running in this year’s race.

This week on InFocus, Pawnee/Ponca lawyer Brett Chapman tells us about the candidates he’s following and how Native Americans are feeling the impact of Trump’s second term.

A recent study by the Brookings Institution reported that the Trump administration slashed $469 million in grants and contracts to tribal communities.

“I think a big problem with the administration, the second go around, is that because of the focus by them on DEI [Diversity, Equity and Inclusion], things of that nature, they have really tried to reduce Native American issues to [being] race-based,” Chapman said.

“What defines being Native American in the United States is not being a member of a race. It’s political sovereignty in the history of over 500 tribes having treaties with the government, and they’re having their own governments. And so you’re having a government-to-government relationship.

title: Columnist says more pressing issues on agenda at First Nations meeting than abolishing Indian Act
content:

title: Federal government says lack of housing on First Nations ‘strictly’ a funding issue
content:
During the final hour of a two-day hearing at the Federal Court of Appeal, lawyers representing First Nations and Canada argued whether the matter of water and housing on reserve land was about money or human rights.

Canada asserted that when it comes to providing housing, the government “is limited” to providing funding for the homes, making the issue a matter of financial duty.

“First Nations manage their own housing,” said one of Canada’s lawyers. “Leadership determines what is to be built, where it is to be built, and how it will be contained.”

However, lawyers representing Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point First Nations asked how that could be possible, when the Indian Act had caused the housing shortages that are affecting Indigenous communities in the first place.

“There’s such extreme harm that we can say that there’s no way a First Nation would have brought this on itself if it could have afforded it,” said Michael Rosenberg, one of an equally plentiful team of lawyers representing the Nations.

The federal government had recently appealed two decisions made by Federal Court Justice Paul Favel in December 2025, when he had concluded that Canada had the obligation to provide Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point First Nations access to housing and clean drinking water.

“The lawsuit at its heart is about funding and increased funding, not an abstract separation of right,” said a lawyer representing the Liberal government on Wednesday.

Over a phone call, Rosenberg also confirmed to APTN News that, in alignment with that claim, the government was also asking for court costs alongside the appeals.

Back in court, he said the communities were not able to properly provide for themselves without financial and structural support from the government, and Canada did, in fact, still have control over all of the houses on a reserve.

“Part of what has kept these First Nations in this state [of poor housing] has been Canada’s part in the Indian Act, constructed to deprive them,” he said.

Rosenberg argued that according to a report from the Auditor General of Canada submitted to Parliament in 2024, Canada was still in the process of transferring control of housing back to the First Nations.

In the report he referenced that the auditor general had also concluded that, “We found that Indigenous Services Canada was at the early stages of transferring control of housing to First Nations, but no overarching policy framework was in place to guide the department’s work in transferring its programs to First Nations communities.

“Under the Department of Indigenous Services Act,” the report continued, “Indigenous Services Canada is mandated to work with First Nations to gradually transfer departmental responsibilities to First Nations, including housing. As of 31 March 2023, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation did not have the legislative mandate to transfer its responsibilities to First Nations.”

The report also stated that this transfer process “is not imposed” on the First Nations, and they need to want to take over those responsibilities.

Rosenberg said many communities have not expressed that interest because they “aren’t able to provide that support,” without money from Canada.

He said, according to evidence from the original lawsuit, the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) even “resisted the idea of moving Canada’s commitment to First Nations,” which he described as “divesting itself [Canada] of its own commitment.”

Instead, the AFN, a political organization that represents more than 600 First Nations in Canada, has been developing a National First Nations Housing and Infrastructure Strategy, which is a lengthy transition period done in collaboration with ISC, since 2018.

The proposed strategy would include transferring control of funding as well.

“The success of any recognition of First Nations complete authority over their housing depends on a federal initiative to transfer control of housing programs and services funds that is broadly flexible enough to accommodate the wide range of First Nations preferences,” the national organization stated in a release.

This is in part due to “circular funding,” he said, as the government will fund housing projects that require rent, and the rent then paid to the government by members will be dollars collected from government checks.

“That is the dynamic here, however it is dressed up,” he said.

As of 2025, the AFN was still “urging the federal government to honour its intent to transfer control of the First Nations Housing Market Fund (the Fund) to First Nations control,” in order to properly assume control over housing as a whole.

Although Canada has retained that funding, lawyers representing the government said housing is otherwise out of their hands.

“Canada does not dispute the importance of housing, which is why [it] has put billions of dollars towards funding on reserve,” one of its lawyers said. “My friend’s submissions today leave this Court with the impression that the record suggests that Canada does, in fact say who can build, what can build, but respectfully that is not the case.”

The lawyer said “There is a shared responsibility … Not simply the system which Canada determines, it’s a framework that involves consultation at a policy level.”

The three Federal Justices have yet to make a determination.

title: Federal drinking water lawsuit ‘not a case of government spending,’ says lawyer
content:
A lawyer representing Shamattawa First Nation says that if Canada is in control of what’s being built on reserve land, then it would also be responsible for addressing the needs related to clean drinking water and housing.

“If you don’t take Canada’s money, the infrastructure does not get built, does not get operated, does not get maintained,” said defense lawyer Michael Rosenburg, during a hearing in the Federal Court of Appeal on Wednesday in Winnipeg. “That is the dynamic, because these First Nations have been put in this position of dependence.”

In December 2025, Federal Court Justice Paul Favel determined that, in his rulings for two separate class-action lawsuits from Shamattawa and St. Theresa First Nations, that Canada had the obligation to provide these communities with access to housing and clean drinking water.

In one of the decisions, Favel said that the federal government “exerted direct control over every facet of First Nations life through legislations, regulations, policies, and practices since at least the 1880s,” and that “this extends to matters such as water infrastructure.”

However, Canada had appealed that decision, arguing that the lawsuit is based on policy and funding issues rather than a legally binding duty.

During the first of a two-day hearing, a team of lawyers representing the federal government argued that because First Nations are self-governed, they would then be responsible for their own water treatment. Additionally, because Canada was not responsible for the water itself, the 2025 lawsuits were based on funding for infrastructure, which Canada has provided.

Therefore, the government would have no obligation to solve the problems themselves.

The government also argued that Favel had referred to previous cases when making his determination, which had concerned restrictions or decisions that would have interfered with people’s access to resources such as drinking water, “which left open the possibility that a positive obligation could exist, but did not go as far as recognize the general duty.”

Canada’s lawyers called the obligation an “assertion,” which they said Favel backed with no new evidence beyond historical issues such as the impact of colonialism on First Nations, which face these barriers.

Another argument made by Canada was that experts used in the original cases were not reliable.

An example of this claim was Lawrence Reynolds, a retired doctor who had been consulted on the subject of drinking water, who had been “expressly and improperly charged with determining Canada had control over water.”

This was because “water is not fixed and immovable; water migrates, it moves from place to place,” a lawyer said.

Canada also pointed to the Constitution Act, which, according to section 35, “recognizes and affirms the existing Aboriginal and treaty rights of the Aboriginal peoples of Canada,” including the right to “responsibly spend funds,” lawyers said, meaning money which would be allocated to repairing water treatment plants on traditional land.

Rosenburg said making the case about funding undermines the human rights concerns brought up by the communities in the original lawsuits.

“When you exercise such close control, it does not allow Canada to say that when something goes wrong, First Nations have full responsibility,” he said, adding that Canada has full control over infrastructure on First Nations, down to the “colour of the pipes.”

“Class members are between a rock and hard place because the defendant put them there,” he said.

Rosenburg said that Favel had written about the “core of the relationship” between First Nations peoples and Canada, which is “creating a systemic disadvantage by confining them to remote and economic reserves where they’re dependent on Canada to make those lands livable,” and then “imposing restrictions on what they can do to live on reserve from both a regulatory and a fiscal perspective.”

He said this is what would separate the case from “ordinary government spending.”

“You heard my friends reference self-governance, the importance of ensuring that First Nations can govern their own affairs. But that cannot be an excuse to tell First Nations that they must make ends meet when they’re still subject to this [relationship] and they haven’t been restored to a position where they have the resources and the control to make their reserve livable.

“Now ultimately, Canada’s role in creating and maintaining class members’ disadvantage will be critical to delineating the extent of the federal government’s obligations. Recognized class members do not call for unlimited government liability. They do not call for guaranteed outcomes. What they ask is the care to make reasonable efforts to assist to the extent that it is responsible for their inability to realize the promise of a reserve as a livable homeland.”

According to the Indigenous Services website, there are 39 drinking water advisories in Canada from Newfoundland and Labrador to Alberta. The majority of them are in Ontario, where another lawsuit was launched against the federal government. Six of them are in Manitoba.

In 2015, the Liberal government promised to end all water advisories.

The court is scheduled to resume Thursday morning.

Now a 20-year-old plaintiff in Canada’s first youth-led climate trial, Vipond described experiencing catastrophic floods in Calgary in 2013 that the city says resulted in mass evacuations, one death and $6 billion in financial losses.

The trial that began Monday heard in an opening statement from the youths’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”




She said the Charter must protect youth from their own government’s actions.




Vipond told the court on Tuesday that she had experienced several climate change events since the floods, including wildfire smoke and intense heat.

title: Nearly 200 First Nations leaders, the prime minister and premiers gathered for a historic meeting about almost everything. Now what?
content:
The John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive was perhaps, in its own imperfect way, a fitting place for nearly 200 First Nations leaders, most of the country’s premiers and a prime minister to hold a meeting First Nations have wanted for more than a century.




It’s actually two buildings mashed together: a modern glass construction, like a church nave, that lets light pour in from above and gives the hallways a sense of something sacred, while behind it, the old city hall rises as a plain grey slab, a maze of stairs leading to small, dark meeting rooms. 




Outside, the chief set up teepees that strangely echo the building’s peaks.




Three very different structures, sharing the same address.




“This is the first time in 119 years of Crown-First Nations relations that a first ministers meeting has focused solely on First Nations,” Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak, the national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has said many times leading up to the meeting and it’s a line she would repeat at the gathering.

title: Cowichan Tribes to propose solution protecting private property in January: lawyer
content:
The lawyer for the Cowichan Tribes said they will make a proposal in January that protects private property rights in the landmark Aboriginal title case that the B.C. Conservatives have said calls into question who controls British Columbia.




Lawyer David Rosenberg said that if it has “the right attitude,” the incoming Conservative government will find it easier to resolve the Cowichan case than to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, known as 

DRIPA

.




The 2025 Cowichan ruling on a portion of Crown, city and private land in Richmond, B.C., found that Aboriginal title is a “senior interest” compared with fee-simple title, and sections of B.C.’s Land Title Act that establish fee-simple title as “indefeasible” do not apply to Aboriginal title.




It has triggered concerns about the impact on private property rights and values, but Rosenberg said the tribes will go to court in the new year with a solution to respect and protect private property and its value, as well as Cowichan Aboriginal title.

He said the case has nothing to do with the repeal of DRIPA, which premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has said is his top priority after Saturday’s election victory.

title: Canada appeals landmark rulings that found it has legal duties on First Nations water and housing
content:
Chiefs from Shamattawa, St. Theresa Point and Sandy Lake First Nations return to court this week to defend landmark Federal Court decisions that recognized Canada’s legal duties to provide safe drinking water and adequate housing on reserve — rulings the Carney government is appealing.

“The Government of Canada continues to fight us in Court over one of our most basic rights as human beings,” said Chief Jordna Hill of Shamattawa First Nation. “But Canada knows what it has done to First Nations people is wrong.”

“Canada ships bottled water to reserves for their federal employees, while First Nations people living under long-term drinking water advisories are forced to use the contaminated tap water.”

The two court cases in question that the Federal Government is appealing are Shamattawa First Nation v. Canada [Water] and St. Theresa Point First Nation v. Canada [Housing].

In those decisions, he ruled that Canada owes fiduciary duties, a common law duty of care, and Charter rights to equality, life, liberty and security of the person, and religion in relation to on-reserve drinking water and housing.

title: Treaty One opens campus to the first national First Nations business training centre
content:
The CEO of a First Nations-led centre for business education and mentorship says that her goal is to shift the narrative so that Indigenous Peoples are not seen as “recipients,” but “creators and innovators” of wealth and services.

WTEC was founded in May 2025, but did not have a physical location until Tuesday.

“When we talk about First Nations economic development, it usually starts with what we lack,” Bluesky said at the grand opening event. “We lack capital, we lack capacity, we lack opportunities. “We bring knowledge, we bring our relationships, and we bring our determination, and we show up,” she continued. “And we’ve been providing for our people, our families, our communities, for generations, and we will continue to do so.”

She said, “aside from the paint on the walls,” the space, located on the third floor of 191 Broadway St. in downtown Winnipeg, was funded entirely by First Nations startups who have benefited from services at WTEC since its inception.

title: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun says it’s up to citizens to decide how to move forward on Eagle mine
content:
The First Nation at the centre of the Eagle gold mine disaster in north-central Yukon says it will ultimately be up to its citizens to decide how it plans to support the sale of the mine to a foreign mining company.

The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, on whose traditional territory the mine is located, indicated in an Oct. 23 news release that while negotiations with Singapore-based mining and acquisitions company Boroo are in the early stages, the relationship appears positive.

“Boroo has approached our Nation with openness, respect and good faith, and we recognize the positive foundation that has been established,” it says.

“We are not turning away from mining. We believe the answer is to do it better,” it adds.

The release says the First Nation is not granting any interviews for the time being.

A failure at the mine’s heap leach facility in June 2024 saw more than 300,000 cubic metres of cyanide-contaminated water released into the surrounding environment on the First Nation’s traditional territory. The mine subsequently went into receivership.

The Yukon government and PricewaterhouseCoopers, the mine’s receiver, announced last week that they had reached an agreement to sell the mine for up to $140 million, a process they said will include input from Na-Cho Nyäk Dun.

title: Atikamekw baby to be reburied in home community more than 70 years after death
content:
More than 70 years after his death, an Atikamekw baby buried far from his family in Quebec City will be laid to rest in his home community.




After 12 years of searching, the family of Maxime Ottawa has located his burial site, exhumed his remains and confirmed his identity, bringing what relatives describe as “immense relief.”




“On Oct. 26, 2026, Baby Maxime will finally come home to Manawan, to his mother and father, to his brothers and sisters,” his niece, Manon Ottawa, said Thursday at a news conference in Montreal.




Maxime was the brother of her father, Henri Ottawa, whose wish to find out what happened to the child prompted her to begin searching in 2014.




Manawan is an Atikamekw community located about 250 kilometres north of Montreal.




In 1954, when Maxime was just six months old, he was taken from Manawan to La Tuque, Que., for medical treatment without his parents.




He was later transferred to Quebec City without his family being informed. He died on Oct. 5, 1954, after 43 days in the hospital, without his loved ones having the chance to see him one last time.




His parents only learned of his death two years later and were unable to hold a funeral or bury him according to their traditions and beliefs.




“In 2014, four years after the death of my father Henri, I began searching, according to his wishes, to find my uncle,” Ottawa told reporters.
